intro/hello: This lecture is about looking inside a trained ConvNet.
intro/cat: Show this small one a photo, and it answers: cat, ninety seven percent sure.
intro/how: But how did it decide? The answer is spread over thirty six thousand numbers, and reading them one by one tells you almost nothing.
intro/toolbox: So between twenty thirteen and twenty fifteen, researchers built a toolbox for looking inside.
intro/why: Why look? To debug a model that keys on the wrong evidence, like a background or a watermark. To trust it. And for science: what did it discover on its own?
intro/tools: We will see its weights and activations, maps of which pixels matter, images it dreams up, and one deeply unsettling discovery.
intro/clue: One warning: each tool answers one narrow question. Treat every picture as a clue, not an explanation.
network/one: Every picture in this lecture comes from one small network, trained on see-far ten, the same one from start to finish.
network/input: Its input is a thirty two by thirty two color image, minus the average color.
network/blocks: Then come three blocks of the same three steps. First, a convolution with a bank of filters: sixteen, then thirty two, then sixty four.
network/relu: Then a ray-loo, which zeroes every negative number. And max pooling, which halves the height and the width.
network/code: What is left, sixty four maps of four by four, is the image's CNN code: a thousand and twenty four numbers.
network/fc: One last layer turns it into ten class scores. On test images, the network is right eighty two percent of the time.
network/cache: Forward keeps every intermediate result in a cache, so we can look at any layer.
network/bwd: And a second call backpropagates all the way to the pixels: one slope per input value, saying how fast the output changes with it.
network/two: Every tool in this lecture is built from these two calls.
activations/what: First, the most direct view: what each layer computes for one image.
activations/filter: Take one first-layer filter: a block of weights, seven by seven pixels, times three colors.
activations/dot: Lay it on a patch of the image, multiply each weight by the pixel under it, and add up the products: a match score.
activations/slide: The ray-loo keeps only positive matches. Slide the filter everywhere, and you paint a map of where its pattern appears.
activations/maps: Sixteen filters, sixteen maps: the layer's activations, or feature maps. In conv1 they still look like the photo.
activations/deeper: Conv2's maps are coarser and more selective. Conv3's, eight by eight, are mostly dark.
activations/sparse: Across the test set, half of conv1's values are zero, and eighty percent of conv3's. Deep units fire only for what they detect.
activations/dead: A map that stays black for every image means a dead filter: its ray-loo never opens, so it never learns again. This network has none.
filters/weights: Weights, unlike activations, do not depend on the image. And first-layer weights look straight at pixels.
filters/draw: So each filter is itself a tiny seven by seven color picture, and we can just draw it.
filters/init: Before training: random noise, and eleven percent accuracy, which is chance.
filters/steps: After a hundred steps, accuracy is forty six percent, yet the filters still look like noise.
filters/epochs: After three epochs they turn smooth, and by thirty, two families stand out.
filters/edges: Oriented edge detectors: light and dark bars at different angles.
filters/blobs: And color blobs: one color against its opposite.
filters/alex: Alex net's first layer shows the same two families. Smooth, clean filters like these mean a network trained well. Noisy ones mean it needs more training, or more regularization.
filters/deeper: Deeper filters weigh feature maps, not pixels, so for them we look at what they respond to instead.
top-images/idea: Pick one unit deep in the network, run twelve hundred images through it, and keep the ones that make it fire hardest.
top-images/ch20: Channel twenty of the last pooling layer: its top eight are all cars.
top-images/rf: A deep unit sees only part of the image, its receptive field, boxed here in yellow.
top-images/space: But think of the layer's output at one spot as a point in sixty four dimensions. Channel twenty is just one axis of that space.
top-images/random: Szegedy and colleagues tried random directions instead: random mixes of all the channels.
top-images/same: Their top images look just as coherent. This one is mostly horses.
top-images/count: On average, a channel's top eight share a label four point one times, a random direction's four point oh times, and chance gives two point four.
top-images/meaning: So single neurons are not special. The meaning lives in the space the whole layer spans.
tsne/code: To see the whole representation at once, take each image's CNN code: the thousand and twenty four numbers of the last pooling layer.
tsne/close: Codes that lie close together belong to images the network finds similar.
tsne/squash: Tee snee squashes them down to two dimensions, sliding points around until neighbors in the big space are neighbors on the page.
tsne/map: Here are a thousand images at their spots. Vehicles gather in one region, animals in another, with planes and ships near the sky and water.
tsne/pixels: Embed the raw pixels instead, and the map sorts by color and brightness, not by meaning.
tsne/nn: This horse's six nearest neighbors in code space are all horses. In pixel space: planes, birds, and a cat.
tsne/count: Overall, a code-space neighbor shares the label fifty five percent of the time, a pixel-space neighbor twenty six percent.
tsne/caveat: One caution: in such a map, the gaps between far-apart clusters mean little.
occlusion/ask: Here is a question for any classifier, no insides needed: if I hide part of the image, does the prediction suffer?
occlusion/patch: Zeiler and Fergus covered a small square with gray: zeros, since the average color was already subtracted.
occlusion/record: Run the network, and record its probability for the true class, bird.
occlusion/slide: Slide the square across, two pixels at a time, and paint each probability into a map.
occlusion/read: Yellow: the network hardly noticed. Dark purple: covering that spot hurt the most, so the network relied on it.
occlusion/cost: It is honest and easy to explain, but costly: one forward pass per position, two hundred and fifty six here.
occlusion/next: Saliency maps get a similar answer from a single backward pass.
saliency/local: Simonyan and colleagues asked it locally: if one pixel changed a tiny bit, how much would the class score change?
saliency/deriv: That is a derivative: the score's slope as you wiggle one input, holding the rest still.
saliency/one: One backward pass gives all three thousand and seventy two. Set the score gradient to one for our class, zero elsewhere, and backpropagate.
saliency/abs: Keep each slope's size, the largest over the three colors, and you have the saliency map.
saliency/look: It is speckled, but it mostly sits on the dog, not the background.
saliency/relu: Two variants change only how the backward pass crosses each ray-loo.
saliency/grad: The true gradient passes the signal wherever the unit was active going forward.
saliency/deconv: Zeiler and Fergus's deconvnet passes it wherever the incoming gradient is positive.
saliency/guided: Guided backpropagation demands both, and draws a crisp outline of the dog.
saliency/but: But crisp is not faithful. Ask guided backprop to explain cat instead, and its map barely changes.
saliency/corr: Across two hundred images, guided maps of two classes correlate at zero point six eight, plain gradients at zero point three eight. Sharpness can come from the image's edges, not the network's reasoning.
class-viz/turn: Now turn the question around, and ask the network to draw.
class-viz/which: Which image makes the deer score as large as possible?
class-viz/ascent: Start from near gray and run gradient ascent on the pixels: training's gradient descent, except the weights stay fixed, the image changes, and we climb.
class-viz/raw: We climb the raw score, since a probability can also rise by pushing the other classes down.
class-viz/penalty: An L two penalty, lambda times the image's squared size, keeps pixels from running to garish extremes.
class-viz/tricks: Three more tricks tame the noise. Blur every ten steps. Jitter the image a pixel or two before each step, and back after. And clip, so pixels stay valid colors.
class-viz/watch: Within ten steps the network is over ninety nine percent sure, yet the picture keeps sharpening, because the raw score keeps climbing.
class-viz/strip: Even this small network paints parts: deer grow antlers, horses grow legs, cars get wheels, and ships sit on blue water.
inversion/remember: How much does a layer's code remember? Mahendran and Vedaldi inverted it to find out.
inversion/search: Starting from noise, search for an image whose code matches the original's.
inversion/descend: This time we descend, on the squared mismatch, scaled by the target's size.
inversion/inject: Its gradient at that layer is twice the difference, and backward to image carries it down to the pixels, plus a small smoothness penalty.
inversion/conv1: From conv1, the image comes back almost perfectly.
inversion/conv2: From conv2, the layout and colors survive, a little smeared.
inversion/deep: From conv3 and pool3, parts land roughly in place, but colors and textures drift.
inversion/invariance: The network throws away details that do not matter for classification. That growing invariance is exactly what a classifier needs.
dream-style/dream: In twenty fifteen, Google gave this a playful twist, soon nicknamed deep dream.
dream-style/amplify: Instead of a class, ask the image to amplify whatever a layer already sees, by injecting its activations as their own gradient.
dream-style/grows: Our tiny network grows stripes and round, eye-like spots. Google's big one grew dogs and pagodas out of clouds.
dream-style/style: Gatys and colleagues used the same machinery to split an image into content and style.
dream-style/content: Content is a deep layer's feature maps, which, as inversion showed, keep the layout.
dream-style/gram: Style is a Gram matrix: for every pair of feature maps, multiply them position by position, and add it all up.
dream-style/where: It is big when two features fire together, like stripes and orange, but the sum forgets where.
dream-style/texture: Start from noise and match the frog's Gram matrices. Its colors and textures return, scrambled: the frog itself is gone.
dream-style/transfer: Style transfer adds a content term for a photo, so the photo keeps its layout and takes on an artwork's textures.
fooling/find: Szegedy and colleagues found that almost any correctly classified image can be changed, invisibly, into any wrong class.
fooling/try: Let us try. This deer is classified correctly. Target: plane.
fooling/step: Nudge every pixel a quarter of a brightness level, in the direction that raises the plane score.
fooling/stop: Repeat until the network says plane.
fooling/done: Thirteen steps. No pixel moved by more than about three levels out of two hundred and fifty five, so the pictures look identical.
fooling/transfer: Worse, such images often fool other networks too, even ones trained on different data.
fooling/reverse: And Nguyen and colleagues found the reverse: noise-like images that networks call an object with over ninety nine percent confidence.
linear/guess: Why? The first guess was that deep networks are too nonlinear.
linear/opposite: Goodfellow, Shlens and Szegedy argued the opposite: they are too linear.
linear/setup: Take a linear score, W dot x, and nudge every input by a tiny epsilon, toward its weight's sign.
linear/tiny: Two levels out of two hundred and fifty five: invisible.
linear/adds: But every nudge helps, so they add up instead of canceling: the score rises by epsilon times the total weight size.
linear/grows: That rise grows with the number of inputs, n, while the score's natural spread grows only like the square root of n.
linear/big: At ten inputs the nudge is lost. At see-far ten size it matches the spread, and at ImageNet size it is over eight spreads.
linear/fgsm: ConvNets are built from piecewise linear parts, so the same trick works: one epsilon step along the sign of the loss gradient. The fast gradient sign method.
linear/panda: Its famous example turns a panda into a gibbon, at ninety nine percent confidence.
linear/matters: Anyone who controls the input can attack a model, and linear classifiers fall the same way. Adversarial training helps, but robustness stayed an open problem.
closing/health: Activations and first-layer filters: the cheapest health check.
closing/meaning: Top images and tee snee: the network groups by meaning, and single neurons are not special.
closing/where: Occlusion and saliency: which parts a decision depends on.
closing/draw: Gradient steps on the pixels: class pictures, inversion, deep dream and style.
closing/fool: And the same gradient, turned against the network, finds adversarial examples.
closing/clue: Each picture is a clue, not an explanation.
closing/next: Next, conv nets in practice: how to make one work on a real problem, with little data and a real budget.
